questions.problem: Consider the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\,1-3t,\,5+6t⟩$, $t\ge 0$, for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=7t.$ Find $R(s),$ the parametrization of the curve by its arc length $s.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $s=7t$, we have that $t=\frac{s}{7}.$

The vector function that pametrizes the curve $r(t)$ by its arc length $s$, with $s\ge 0$, is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{7}) \\  & =⟨2(\frac{s}{7}),\,1-3(\frac{s}{7}),\,5+6(\frac{s}{7})⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{7}⟨2s,\,7-3s,\,35+6s⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve $r(t)=3t\,i+2{t}^{3/2}\,j+4\,k,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by  $s=2(1+t)^{3/2}-2.$ Given that $R(s)$ is the parameterization of the given curve by its arc length $s,$ what is the $y$-component of $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $s=2(1+t)^{3/2}-2$, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =2(1+t)^{3/2}-2 \\ s+2 & =2(1+t)^{3/2} \\ \frac{s+2}{2} & =(1+t)^{3/2} \\ {(\frac{s}{2}+1)}^{2/3} & =1+t \\ t & ={(\frac{s}{2}+1)}^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r({(\frac{s}{2}+1)}^{2/3}-1) \\  & =3[{(\frac{s}{2}+1)}^{2/3}-1]\,i+2{[{(\frac{s}{2}+1)}^{2/3}-1]}^{3/2}\,j+4\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the $y$-component of $R$ is

$$
2{[{(\frac{s}{2}+1)}^{2/3}-1]}^{3/2}.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve $r(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s={e}^{t}-1.$ Given that $R(s)$ is the parametrization of the given curve by its arc length $s,$ what is the $x$-component of $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $s={e}^{t}-1,$ we have that $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1).$

The vector function that pametrizes the curve $r(t)$ by its arc length $s,$ with $s\ge 0,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)}\operatorname{sin}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)],\,{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)}\operatorname{cos}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)]⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(s+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)],\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(s+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)]⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the $x$-component of $R$ is

$$
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(s+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)].

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Unit Tangent Given the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
questions.problem: Given the curve  $r(t)=⟨2{e}^{t},\,3{e}^{t},\,6{e}^{t}⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=7({e}^{t}-1),$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $s=7({e}^{t}-1)$, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{s}{7} & ={e}^{t}-1 \\ {e}^{t} & =\frac{s}{7}+1 \\ t & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})) \\  & =⟨2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})},\,3{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})},\,6{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{s+7}{7})}⟩ \\  & =⟨2\cdot \frac{s+7}{7},\,3\cdot \frac{s+7}{7},\,6\cdot \frac{s+7}{7}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2s+14}{7},\,\frac{3s+21}{7},\,\frac{6s+42}{7}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2s+14}{7}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3s+21}{7}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{6s+42}{7})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{7},\,\frac{3}{7},\,\frac{6}{7}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve  $r(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+6t\,k,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=10t,$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $s=10t$, we have that $t=\frac{s}{10}.$

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{10}) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{10})i+8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{10})j+6(\frac{s}{10})k \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{10})i+8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{10})j+\frac{3s}{5}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{s}{10})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{s}{10})j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3s}{5})k \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{10})i+8\cdot \frac{1}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{10})j+\frac{3}{5}\,k \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{10})i+\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{10})j+\frac{3}{5}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
questions.problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{4},\,\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+2,\,3-{t}^{4}⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-{t}^{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3},\,2{t}^{3},\,-4{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =2{t}^{3}⟨2,\,1,\,-2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|2{t}^{3}|\sqrt{{(2)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =2{t}^{3}\sqrt{4+1+4} \\  & =6{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}6{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{t}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{u}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}$ and $t\ge 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4} & =s \\ {t}^{4} & =\frac{2s}{3} \\ t & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}}) \\  & =⟨{(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{4},\,\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{4}+2,\,3-{(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2s}{3},\,\frac{s}{3}+2,\,3-\frac{2s}{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2s,\,s+6,\,9-2s⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
questions.problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{4})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{4})\,j,$  $\,t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{4}))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{4}))j \\  & =-4{t}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{4})\,i+4{t}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{4})\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{[-4{t}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{4})]}^{2}+{[4{t}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{4})]}^{2}} \\  & =4|t{|}^{3}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡({t}^{4})+{cos}^{2}⁡({t}^{4})} \\  & =4{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}4{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={u}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={t}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $s={t}^{4}$, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{4} & =s \\ t & =\sqrt[4]{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt[4]{s}) \\  & =cos\,((\sqrt[4]{s})^{4})\,i+sin\,((\sqrt[4]{s})^{4})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(s)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(s)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
questions.problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{t}{2},\,\frac{t}{2},\,t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{2},\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\cdot u{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,t\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,t$,  we have that $t=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s.$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s,\,\frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s,\,\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,s⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{6}\,s}{6},\,\frac{\sqrt{6}\,s}{6},\,\frac{\sqrt{6}\,s}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
questions.problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3,\,t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0,\,-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}} \\  & =|t| \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ we have that $t=\sqrt{2s}.$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{2s}) \\  & =⟨\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{2s}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{2s},\,3,\,\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{2s}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{2s}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the parametrization of the curve $r(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ by its arc length $s?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{2}}|\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & ={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s={e}^{t}-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}-1 & =s \\ {e}^{t} & =s+1 \\ t & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)}\operatorname{cos}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)],\,{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)}\operatorname{sin}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)]⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-(s+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)],\,(s+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)]⟩ \\  & =\frac{s+1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)],\,\operatorname{sin}⁡[\operatorname{ln}⁡(s+1)]⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length Given Its Arc Length
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the curve  $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle 2t-1 ,\: 8t+2 ,\: -2t \right\rangle, \, t \geq 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $\mathbf{r}(0)$ to $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is given by $s=6\sqrt{2}t.$ Find $\mathbf R(s),$ the parametrization of the curve by its arc length $s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, since  $s=6\sqrt{2}t,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}6\sqrt{2}t & =s \\ t & =\frac{s}{6\sqrt{2}} \\ t & =\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

The vector function that pametrizes the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ by its arc length $s,$ with $s \geq 0,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{12}) \\  & =⟨2(\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{12})-1,\,8(\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{12})+2,\,-2(\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{12})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{6}-1,\,\frac{4\sqrt{2}s}{6}+2,\,-\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{6}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{6}⟨\sqrt{2}s-6,\,4\sqrt{2}s+12,\,-\sqrt{2}s⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Unit Tangent Given the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
canonical_examples.problem: Given the curve  $\mathbf r(t)=\cos{t}\,\mathbf i - \sin{t}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{3}t\,\mathbf k, \, t \geq 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $\mathbf r(0)$ to $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by $s=2t,$ find the corresponding unit tangent $\mathbf{T}(s),$ parametrized by $s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, since $s=2t,$ we have that $t=\dfrac{s}{2}.$

Therefore, the vector function $\mathbf R(s)$ that parametrizes $\mathbf r(t)$ by its arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{s}{2}k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}s}{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s,$ the unit tangent can be found as

$$
\mathbf T(s) = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}s}\mathbf R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2}))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2}))j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{3}s}{2})k \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{2})\,j+\sqrt{3}\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametrization of a Curve by Arc Length
canonical_examples.problem: What is the parametrization of the curve  $\mathbf r(t)=2(t\cos{t}-\sin{t})\,\mathbf i+2(t\sin{t}+\cos{t})\,\mathbf j, \, t \geq 0$ by its arc length $s?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and its magnitude $\|\mathbf{r}'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|2t|\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we removed the absolute value bars since $t>0.$ 

Next, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}2u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={t}^{2}-0 \\  & ={t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $s=t^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =s \\ t & =\pm \sqrt{s} \\ t & =\sqrt{s},\end{aligned}
$$

taking the positive root because $t>0.$  

Finally, the vector function that parametrizes $\mathbf r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{s}) \\  & =2(\sqrt{s}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s})\,i+2(\sqrt{s}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s})\,j.\end{aligned}
$$
